name: polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
aliases: pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy

clinicalPearls: Typically arises in the third trimester (or immediately postpartum) in a primigravida, and characteristically begins within abdominal striae distensae.
The periumbilical region is spared, an important clinical clue distinguishing it from pemphigoid gestationis which frequently involves the umbilicus.
Lesions are polymorphic: urticarial papules and plaques predominate but vesicles, targetoid lesions, eczematous change and widespread erythema may all occur.
Strongly associated with excessive maternal weight gain, multiple gestation (twins, triplets) and male fetal sex.
It is a clinical diagnosis; direct immunofluorescence is negative and is used mainly to exclude pemphigoid gestationis when in doubt.
Intensely pruritic but self-limiting, usually resolving within a few weeks of delivery without scarring.
There is no associated maternal or fetal risk, distinguishing it prognostically from intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and pemphigoid gestationis.
First-line management is emollients and topical corticosteroids with oral antihistamines; a short course of systemic corticosteroid is reserved for severe cases.
reference.pathophysiology: The aetiology is incompletely understood but is thought to relate to rapid abdominal wall distension in the third trimester causing damage to connective tissue within striae, exposing altered collagen that provokes an inflammatory response. This is supported by the strong associations with excessive weight gain, large fetal size and multiple gestation. A contribution from circulating fetal DNA and a mild immunological reaction to fetal antigens has been proposed, and the male-fetus association raises the possibility of a response to fetal cells in maternal skin, but no consistent hormonal or autoimmune mechanism has been confirmed. Unlike pemphigoid gestationis there is no autoantibody to the basement membrane zone.
additionalInvestigations: skin biopsy for histology (non-specific: dermal oedema with perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate and eosinophils)
direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin (negative, to exclude pemphigoid gestationis)
serum bile acids and liver function tests to exclude obstetric cholestasis
full blood count (eosinophilia may occur but is non-specific)
indirect immunofluorescence or BP180 ELISA if pemphigoid gestationis is suspected
obstetric ultrasound to confirm multiple gestation and fetal wellbeing
redFlags: periumbilical involvement or tense blisters suggesting pemphigoid gestationis rather than polymorphic eruption
pruritus without primary skin lesions plus dark urine or pale stools, raising intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
jaundice or right upper quadrant pain suggesting hepatic pathology
reduced fetal movements or other signs of fetal compromise
systemic upset, fever or mucosal involvement suggesting an alternative severe dermatosis or drug reaction
reference.prognosis: Excellent, with spontaneous resolution typically within one to six weeks of delivery and no scarring. There is no increased maternal or fetal morbidity and recurrence in subsequent pregnancies is uncommon.
pitfalls: Mislabelling any tense blistering as polymorphic eruption; umbilical involvement and positive direct immunofluorescence point to pemphigoid gestationis.
Failing to check bile acids in a pruritic pregnant woman and missing intrahepatic cholestasis, which carries fetal risk.
Assuming recurrence in later pregnancies and causing unnecessary anxiety when recurrence is in fact unusual.
Overusing systemic corticosteroids for a benign self-limiting condition when topical therapy usually suffices.
Attributing the eruption solely to striae and overlooking the strong link with multiple gestation, delaying recognition of a twin pregnancy.
references: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, current edition
British Journal of Dermatology, dermatoses of pregnancy guidance
Ambros-Rudolph CM et al. Specific dermatoses of pregnancy, Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology
management: Symptomatic relief with mid-potency topical corticosteroids as the mainstay for the intense pruritus
Regular emollients and cooling measures to soothe affected skin
Oral antihistamines, favouring pregnancy-appropriate agents such as chlorphenamine, for troublesome itch
A short tapering course of systemic corticosteroids reserved for severe or widespread eruption
Reassurance that the condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving within weeks of delivery without scarring or increased foetal risk
Exclude pemphigoid gestationis (periumbilical sparing, negative direct immunofluorescence) and obstetric cholestasis (serum bile acids) where the diagnosis is uncertain
